sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain any two features of the Permanent Settlement.
questions.answer: (1) Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal and Bihar in 1793. It made the landlord or zamindar deposit a fixed amount of money in the state treasury. In return they were recognised as hereditary owners of land. (2) But, if the zamindar failed to pay the fixed revenue on time his land was sold off to another zamindar. The British stood to benefit from this settlement as the new class of zamindars that emerged became their political allies.

questions.q: Why did the British invest in improving transport in India? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (1) England on the other hand needed railways that connected the raw material producing areas with the exporting ports and to facilitate the movement of British goods to different parts of the country as well as bring raw materials to the ports. (2) They carried British finished goods to markets all over India; British investors also got a guaranteed 5% profit on railway capital.

or.q: Why did the British create a class of English-educated Indians? Give two reasons.
or.answer: (1) They also needed money for trade, projects of the company as well as for the cost of running the administration. The Indians would be ready to work as clerks on low wages while for the same work the British would demand much higher wages. English became the lingua franca of the educated people in India. (2) This class of Indians would be taught to appreciate the culture and opinion of the British. In addition, they would also help to increase the market for British goods. They assumed that a few educated Indians would spread English culture to the masses and that they would be able to rule through this class of educated Indians.

questions.q: Explain any two reasons why the class of moneylenders grew during British rule.
questions.answer: (1) Unfortunately it brought no benefit to the peasants as the British demands were very high. Time bound and excessive demand of revenue by the British government forced the peasants to take loans from the moneylenders. (2) These moneylenders often exploited the peasants by charging high interest rates. They often used unfair means like false accounting, forged signatures and thumb impressions. The new legal system and the policy introduced by the British only helped the moneylenders who were either local merchants or landlords.

questions.q: Why did the British pressurise Indian farmers to cultivate indigo?
questions.answer: (1) Gradually they wanted to conquer the vast territory of India for which they needed a lot of money. Indigo was sent to England and used as a dyeing agent for cloth produced in British towns. (2) Indians were forced to produce indigo and sell it on the conditions dictated by the Britishers. Indigo was grown under a different system where all farmers were compelled to grow it on 3/20th part of their land.

questions.q: Mention two legal measures which helped improve the status of women in British India.
questions.answer: (1) For example, the practice of sati was banned in 1829 by Lord Bentinck, the then Governor General. (2) Widow Remarriage was permitted by a law passed in 1856. Sharda Act was passed in 1929 preventing child marriage.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: How did the British use political power, trade policies and education to strengthen their control over India? Analyse.
questions.answer: (1) With the strong political control, the British were able to monopolise the trade with India. (2) This was done by a system of alliances called the Doctrine of Lapse and Subsidiary Alliance. (3) They wanted to use education as a means to strengthen their political authority in the country.

questions.q: Explain the impact of British trade on the Indian handloom weaving industry.
questions.answer: (1) British machine-made cloth was cheap and entered India without duty, while Indian handicrafts were taxed heavily and Britain put protective tariffs on Indian textiles. (2) Therefore, within a few years, India from being an exporter of clothes became an exporter of raw cotton and an importer of British clothes. From an exporter India became an importer of these goods. In the tea plantations ownership changed hands quite often. (3) Handloom weaving collapsed (de-industrialisation), weavers became unemployed and moved to villages as farm labourers, increasing pressure on agriculture.

questions.q: Why did the British pressurise the cultivation of indigo in India? Explain the reasons for the discontent of the farmers.
questions.answer: (1) Indigo was needed as a dye for British textile mills. Discontent: (2) Indigo was grown under a different system where all farmers were compelled to grow it on 3/20th part of their land. (3) Indians were forced to produce indigo and sell it on the conditions dictated by the Britishers. This meant buying of raw materials at very cheap rates and selling finished goods at much higher prices. (4) Unfortunately cultivation of Indigo left the land infertile for some years. Because the peasants now shifted to commercial crops, food grain production went down.

questions.q: Explain the impact of the British education policy on India.
questions.answer: (1) It was also expected to create a class of Indians who were loyal to the British and were not able to relate to other Indians. The British Parliament issued the Charter Act of 1813 by which a sum of Rupees One lakh was sanctioned for promoting western sciences in India. Another step in this direction was the Woods Despatch of 1854. (2) As part of the directive given by the Woods Despatch, Departments of Education were instituted in all provinces and Affiliated Universities were opened in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in 1857. A few English schools and colleges were opened instead of many elementary schools. (3) . (4) The mass production of goods through machines that we witness today was pioneered through the Industrial Revolution which occurred first in England during the late 18th and the early 19th century. Education soon became a monopoly of the rich and the city dwellers. (5) But English became a link language and Western ideas of liberty, equality and democracy spread, producing reformers and nationalists.

questions.q: Distinguish between the Permanent Settlement and the Mahalwari Settlement.
questions.answer: (1) Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal and Bihar in 1793. This made the zamindar the owner of the land. But, if the zamindar failed to pay the fixed revenue on time his land was sold off to another zamindar. (2) In 1822, the British introduced the Mahalwari Settlement in the North Western Provinces, Punjab, the Ganga Valley and parts of Central India. Here the basis of assessment was the product of a mahal or estate, which may be a village or a group of villages. Here all the proprietors of mahal were jointly responsible for paying the sum of revenue assessed by the government. (3) By 1813, the Indian handicrafts lost both their domestic as well as foreign market. Unfortunately it brought no benefit to the peasants as the British demands were very high.

questions.q: Why did the British seek to restrict the development of India? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) There was a massive import of machine made clothes from English factories to Indian markets. Since ancient times, the main source of livelihood for the people were agriculture. They wanted India to be a part of the modern, progressive world of science. To find raw materials for their industries in Britain and markets for their finished goods. (2) At the same time, they also required a market to sell their finished goods. They now wanted to invest this wealth in setting up industries and trade with India. Indian goods could not compete with the British factory-made products where machines were used. (3) Heavy duties on Indian goods and free entry for British goods protected British industry. These policies drained India's wealth and kept it poor.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the economic impact of British rule on India in six points.
questions.answer: (1) De-industrialisation: cheap, duty-free British cloth ruined Indian handlooms and other crafts. (2) From an exporter India became an importer of these goods. To find raw materials for their industries in Britain and markets for their finished goods. (3) The Permanent, Mahalwari and Ryotwari settlements imposed very high land revenue, impoverishing peasants. (4) They forced the commercialisation of agriculture with the growing of various cash crops and the raw materials for the industries in the Britain. Another major economic impact of the British policies in India was the introduction of a large number of commercial crops such as tea, coffee, indigo, opium, cotton, jute, sugarcane and oilseed. (5) Peasants fell into debt and lost land to moneylenders; a new middle class of agents and zamindars arose. (6) There was an enormous drain of wealth to Britain through profits, salaries and pensions; railways were built mainly to serve British trade.
